body: I still personally think a static method for this is the best option, it involves the least code hacking to make it work in various cases, it is the most transparent and least confusing what it actually means, it is also far easier to notice in reading code fast, `foo(Vector2(1), 2)` is far harder to read at a glance IMO for example

> I still personally think a static method for this is the best option, it involves the least code hacking to make it work in various cases, it is the most transparent and least confusing what it actually means, it is also far easier to notice in reading code fast, `foo(Vector2(1), 2)` is far harder to read at a glance IMO for example

I see your point, but for source code it’s actually shorter and faster to just use the constructor than to rely on a static method, even if the static one gets inlined. In some of our use cases, the new constructor avoids creating a temporary variable and skips redundant operations.

For scripting languages I agree with you though, it makes more sense not to expose the constructor directly, and instead provide a static wrapper for the single-value case.

I also ran tests with the inlined static method and didn’t observe any performance gain. From what I can tell, it still passes the arguments through to the vector constructor (x and y) and the constructor ends up recalculating them twice anyway.

> Personally I'm still _somewhat_ in favour, because i'm used to tensor broadcasting, which makes "single-argument construction" possible by default — but it's not a clear win.

This was added mainly for internal use, where it helps reduce code size and avoid unnecessary temporaries, giving both cleaner and faster code.

It also matches established conventions: scalar vector constructors are common in math libraries and already supported in shaders. Extending this to C++ keeps the API consistent, while scripting can still rely on a static wrapper if needed.

This general idea being scattered across several issues/Prs makes it a bit hard to keep arguments in one place :slightly_smiling_face:  I'll thus repeat mine from https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/109687#issuecomment-3195457197. Slightly different situation for C++ than GDScript, but the idea is the same.

---

 I believe if this functionality is added, it would be better expressed as a named constructor:
```gdscript
var v = Vector3.splat(4)  # (4, 4, 4)
```
This is more explicit and can be immediately recognized.
It also prevents bugs:
```gdscript
# Used to be 3D, but game logic can be done in 2D -> now migrated
var a: Vector2 = ...
var b: Vector2 = ...

# Forgot to update that 2D cross is float, not vector
var v = a.cross(b)

var tile_coords = Vector2i(v / TILE_SIZE)
# currently: error because float cannot be converted to Vector2i
# with this PR: silently works but yields garbage
```
Note that the above code isn't even dynamically typed -- in those cases it's even more important to highlight "unusual" operations by making them more explicit.

---



> It also matches established conventions: scalar vector constructors are common in math libraries and already supported in shaders. Extending this to C++ keeps the API consistent, while scripting can still rely on a static wrapper if needed.

The ecosystem is split on this. While you're right that many math libraries support single-argument constructors, not all do. Some counterexamples:
- [Bullet Physics](https://pybullet.org/Bullet/BulletFull/classbtVector3.html)
- [SFML](https://www.sfml-dev.org/documentation/3.0.2/classsf_1_1Vector3.html)
- [sdl2pp](https://libsdl2pp.github.io/classSDL2pp_1_1Point.html), C++ wrapper for SDL 2
- [Eigen](https://libeigen.gitlab.io/eigen/docs-nightly/group__QuickRefPage.html) -- `Vector3f::Constant(val)`, see _Predefined Matrices_

Thank you for the feedback!

For this PR, my focus is solely on the engine’s performance in C++. I’ve implemented this feature only in the source code, and I don’t intend to expose it to scripting languages. Whether scripting languages have a similar feature or not is not relevant for this work.

The goal here is to provide a fast, efficient way to construct a vector from a scalar inside the engine, and the considerations about scripting ergonomics don’t affect this.

Please take a look at how GCC, Clang, and MSVC handle the two static methods. Currently, the `from_scalar `method cannot be optimized in the same way as `from_scalar2` on all compilers (except for Clang). Even without optimization (dev_build=yes), it remains relatively slow. https://godbolt.org/z/5oo6WcxTh

To ensure that a `Vector3.splat()` implementation is fast across all compilers, the single-value constructor should be implemented first, and the static method can then call it internally.

Also, in C++ I would prefer using `Vector2(value)` rather than `Vector2::splat(value)` for shorter, cleaner lines. Since these constructors are intended to replace temporary variables we previously used before creating the vector, the static method tends to produce longer and harder-to-read code.

I plan to run another comparison in Godot for the scalar constructor versus the static method using `-O2` in GDScript. So far, I’ve only tested with `dev_build=yes`. On Godbolt, both approaches appear to be optimized similarly, but the constructors are completely removed, with values computed and stored in memory at compile time. I wasn’t able to test runtime values there, so I want to ensure that both approaches will perform equally in `GDScript` when the argument is only known at runtime.

> Please take a look at how GCC, Clang, and MSVC handle the two static methods. Currently, the `from_scalar `method cannot be optimized in the same way as `from_scalar2` on all compilers (except for Clang). Even without optimization (dev_build=yes), it remains relatively slow. https://godbolt.org/z/5oo6WcxTh I swapped the 2 calls to `from_scalar` and `from_scalar2`. The resulting assembly is identical. https://godbolt.org/z/MsEMacrze To make sure it's not just a reordering, I checked the mapping of C++ to Assembly by hovering over with the mouse (you don't see caret in screenshot -- I selected the line, but you can verify by hovering): * `from_scalar` first: * `from_scalar2` first: So the difference must be something else. It would _really_ surprise me if such a basic constructor call cannot be optimized by modern compilers.

I just want to clarify that my focus with this PR is on engine performance in C++, not on exposing this feature to scripting languages. The discussion about GDScript naming and explicitness is interesting, but it’s not the main goal of this work.

I’m still learning, and I very much welcome any constructive feedback on the implementation, rather than just disagreements on how it might be exposed to scripting. My priority here is ensuring the scalar constructor is fast and efficient internally.

I definitely intended my feedback to be constructive, and there's a misunderstanding regarding GDScript.
To clarify my points:
- The explicitness is also helpful for C++, not just scripting. Arguably even more so, since C++ has many different syntaxes for constructor calls. If I'm not overlooking something, this constructor can be called as `{1.2}` or `(Vector2) 1.2`.
- Not all math/gamedev libraries use single-arg-ctor convention, so it's not the only obvious choice.
- So far, the performance benefits of a constructor vs. static method couldn't be demonstrated.

I absolutely see the merit in reducing duplication of arguments, so this PR is on the right track to me -- it's just that I'd personally rather use the [Named Constructor Idiom](https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/More_C%2B%2B_Idioms/Named_Constructor), i.e. a static function. But it's ultimately up to the core team to decide what works best for their everyday work.

Hope that clarifies things! :slightly_smiling_face:

Replaced the constructor with a static method `splat`, since `Vector2::splat(variable)` always makes it explicit that the input is a scalar, whereas `Vector2(variable)` requires additional type checking.

I've said this in other chats where this is being discussed, but all the proposals for constructing vectors from a single element stress that they want it to reduce typing or to match GLSL. This PR does neither. By way of example, users feel that `Vector3(1, 1, 1)` is too much to type, they want to type `Vector3(1)` instead. Unfortunately, `Vector3.splat(1)` is more typing _and_ requires more keyboard travel. So it doesn't solve the problem that lead to the proposals in the first place. 

It's unclear what problem this actually solves. There is no performance benefit. Whether it is more readable or not is arguable IMO it is _less_ readable, both because it relies on users assuming that the single element will be copied n times, and because `splat` is not descriptive at all. I haven't seen that terminology in any other API. And it doesn't reduce typing/boilerplate either. 

To be perfectly blunt, at this point this PR is just adding bloat to the core and making the codebase less readable for contributors.

I'd argue that the main reason is less so amount of typing and more so ease of updating and safety of use, especially as this is for the codebase and not an exposed method, it avoids cases where the argument needs to be stored in a temporary or similar. Also while it's true that for trivial cases `Vector3.splat(1)` *is* shorter for a lot of real world cases it is shorter than the alternative, such as:
* `Vector3(center, center, center)` -> `Vector3::splat(center)`
* `Vector3(longest_axis, longest_axis, longest_axis)` -> `Vector3::splat(longest_axis)`

And especially for cases with temporaries, for example:
* `Vector3::splat(Math::sqrt(double(new_simplex->circum_r2))` from two lines with a temporary

In fact from a glance most of the cases in this PR saves at least a few characters, and several saves dozens

But it is a matter of taste and preference, but I'd say that the main goal is more to reduce duplication, the specific readability would depend on the case of course

---

To be clear I'm personally mixed on this particular change, but I do think it has specific merits, but might be more reasonable to apply it in targeted ways where it replaces messy constructions, but would be good to assess broader opinions on the readability

Just to highlight two things:
1. Readability is naturally a subjective thing. I disagree that this is more readable, but I won't die on that hill. 
2. There have been 4 proposals for this feature and this PR addresses none of them. That isn't strictly an issue if this isn't being exposed to end-users, but it does highlight that we may be missing the point. 

On the point of readability, grabbing a. random example from above:
```
box->set_size(Vector3(2, 2, 2) * p_applied_root_scale);
box->set_size(Vector3::splat(2 * p_applied_root_scale));
```

To someone dropping into the codebase the first is very clear, the size of the box is 2 times the applied root scale in each axis. The second one could mean anything. What axis does splat apply to? Does splat apply any other operation? Perhaps it applies a scaling factor or size limits or something. In order to understand the code, the reader needs to navigate to where splat is defined whereas in the former case, the code speaks for itself. 

IMO this is a place where trying to come up with a clever solution to reduce the amount of code makes the codebase harder to navigate and maintain. 

The best solution for all the above cases IMO is to have a temporary variable i.e.:
```
main_button->draw_circle(Vector2(button_radius * 2, button_radius * 2), button_radius, color); // godot
main_button->draw_circle(Vector2::splat(button_radius * 2), button_radius, color); // this PR

//improved
Vector2 circle_radius = button_radius * 2;
main_button->draw_circle(Vector2::(circle_radius, circle_radius), button_radius, color);
```

I agree that `splat` may not be familiar to many developers, especially newer contributors. To improve readability, I’d suggest alternatives such as `Vector3::filled(x)`, `Vector3::all(x)`, or `Vector3::scaled(x)`. These names make it clearer that the same scalar value is being applied across all components.

Edit: `Vector3::filled(x)` is better for readability, and `Vector3::all(x)` is just shorter but still not clear, so I'd prefer `Vector3::filled(x)` over `Vector3::splat(x)`

Regarding the proposals: most of the debate was about exposing this as a constructor in `GDScript` and `GDExtension`, which sparked a lot of disagreement. To avoid reopening that discussion, this PR is limited to the C++ side. If they'd agree on using a static method instead, we can expose it to scripting languages and finally resolve the open proposals and PRs.

> The best solution for all the above cases IMO is to have a temporary variable i.e.:

This is a valid approach too, one thing to note though: this is harder to standardize and relies on out-of-band docs/guidelines. You see it from the current code, various people have different ideas on a best approach:
- `Vector3(long_expr, long_expr, long_expr)`
- `float a = long_expr; Vector3(a, a, a)`
- `long_expr * Vector3(1, 1, 1)`

A dedicated method `Vector3::fill(a)` does not have this issue: people can directly point to it in reviews without needing to cite a "convention". Once it's known, contributors reading the code recognize the pattern immediately. But I agree there's an initial phase where it may be slightly confusing, although with `fill`/`repeat` naming the risk is more limited.

In Godot’s codebase, methods that return a modified copy are consistently written in the past tense:

```c++
Transform2D::rotated(x); // Returns a rotated copy.

Transform2D::scaled(x); // Returns a scaled copy.
```

So following that pattern, `Vector2::filled(x)` makes more sense than `Vector2::fill(x)`, because it signals `Return a Vector2 filled with x` rather than `Fill this Vector2 with x` for a static method. 

Edit: if we expose it later for scripting languages users may mistakenly use it on a vector directly.
```gdscript
node.scale.fill(x * y)

# Instead of
node.scale = Vector2.filled(x * y)
```
